Sharps, flats, and key signatures

A sharp or a flat changes a note by a semitone, and the key signature at the start of each line changes some notes for the whole piece. If you name the notes without them, many names come out wrong: in G major every F is F♯. This page explains the signs and the rules for how far they reach.

The signs

SignNameWhat it doesExample
♯SharpRaises the note a semitoneF → F♯
♭FlatLowers the note a semitoneB → B♭
♮NaturalCancels a sharp or flat (from the key signature or earlier in the measure)F♯ → F
𝄪Double sharpRaises the note two semitonesF → F𝄪 (sounds as G)
𝄫Double flatLowers the note two semitonesB → B𝄫 (sounds as A)

Key signatures

The sharps or flats right after the clef are the key signature. They apply to every note with that name, in every octave, on every line, until a new key signature appears. They are always written in the same order: sharps F C G D A E B, flats B E A D G C F. So one sharp is always F♯, and two flats are always B♭ and E♭.

Key signatureNotes it changesMajor keyMinor key
none—C majorA minor

4 sharpsF♯ C♯ G♯ D♯E majorC♯ minor
5 sharpsF♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ A♯B majorG♯ minor
6 sharpsF♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ A♯ E♯F♯ majorD♯ minor
7 sharpsF♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ A♯ E♯ B♯C♯ majorA♯ minor
1 flatB♭F majorD minor
2 flatsB♭ E♭B♭ majorG minor
3 flatsB♭ E♭ A♭E♭ majorC minor

5 flatsB♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭D♭ majorB♭ minor
6 flatsB♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭ C♭G♭ majorE♭ minor
7 flatsB♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭ C♭ F♭C♭ majorA♭ minor

Every key signature, the notes it changes, and the major and minor key that use it.

A quick way to name the key: with sharps, the major key is one semitone above the last sharp (last sharp F♯ → G major). With flats, it is the second-to-last flat (B♭ E♭ → B♭ major); one flat is F major.

Accidentals: until the bar line

A sharp, flat, or natural written in front of a note (an accidental) lasts until the end of the measure, for that note at that height. After the bar line the key signature applies again. Two exceptions catch many readers:

  • Ties: a note tied over the bar line keeps its accidental. The note after the bar line is the same sound continued.
  • Courtesy accidentals: many scores repeat a sign in the next measure, sometimes in brackets, as a reminder. It changes nothing.

How the names are written

The sign goes after the name: F♯ (“F sharp”), B♭ (“B flat”). In Do Re Mi it is Fa♯ and Si♭, in Japanese ファ♯ and シ♭. F♯ and G♭ sound the same on a piano but are written differently; the name follows what is written. See the note name chart for other languages.

In Note Namer

Note Namer names each note with its sharp or flat already applied: the key signature, the accidentals earlier in the measure, and ties are all taken into account, so a G major score gets F♯ everywhere. When you transpose, the key signature changes and the names follow the new key. If the key signature itself was read wrong, every name in the piece changes with it; check the first line against the paper (see how to fix reading mistakes).
